title: 9 Effect of N fertilization provided as biosolids on bahiagrass yield and in-situ degradability
content:
Abstract
Biosolids are organic wastewater solids that can be recycled and potentially used as fertilizer after stabilization, which destroys pathogens and reduces vector attraction. In Texas, biosolids are applied to 0.23% of croplands, indicating lack of utilization by producers. Bahiagrass (Paspalum notatum) is a warm season forage that can flourish with low inputs and in poorly managed soils. The objective of this study was to evaluate if pelleted biosolids increase the yield and in-situ degradability of bahiagrass to a similar extent as chemical fertilizer. Biosolids were applied at 0, 45, 90, and 135 kg N/ha and urea at 90 kg N/ha to mowed plots of bahiagrass. After application, bahiagrass was sampled at 3, 5, 7, and 9 weeks. Yield was assessed using a sampling square (50 cm2) and analyzing collected forage for dry matter (DM) then organic matter (OM). In-situ characteristics were determined by incubating samples of bahiagrass in ruminally cannulated beef steers at various timepoints from 0 to 72 h. Rate of passage (kp) was set at 3.2%/h. There was a linear increase (P≤0.01) in OM yield in accordance with N provision, from 1,157 kg OM/ha for 0 kg biosolids N/ha to 1,524 kg OM/ha for 135 kg biosolids N/ha. There was not a significant difference between the isonitrogenous level (90 kg N/ha) of biosolids and urea for OM yield (P=0.49). There was a similar linear increase in CP yield from 0 to 135 kg biosolids N/ha (45%; P≤0.01) with no differences between biosolids and urea applied at 90 kg N/ha (P=0.88). There were neither linear nor quadratic effects of level of N fertilization provided via biosolids on in-situ fractionation of OM (P≥0.12). Further, there were no differences in OM fractionation between biosolids or urea provided at 90 kg N/ha (P≥0.65). The rate of OM degradability (kd) was not affected by level of N fertilization provided as biosolids (P=0.88) nor was there a difference between isonitrogenous levels of biosolids and urea (P=0.54). Finally, OM degradability was not affected by level or source of N fertilization (P≥0.64), averaging 59% across treatments. Ultimately, N provided as biosolids increased OM and CP yield but did not change degradability characteristics of bahiagrass. As there were no differences between isonitrogenous levels of biosolids and urea, these data indicate biosolids can effectively substitute for urea as a fertilizer at the levels assessed in this study. These findings have implications to improve human and ecological health, while also potentially maximizing producers’ productivity and economic viability.
